justification_text:
My point estimates were relatively stable across all three horizons, hovering around 31.35 to 31.50. This reflects a near-term anchoring to the most recent observed price or rate level, with only a modest upward drift built in over time. At the one-day horizon, the estimate is essentially a carry-forward of current conditions with minimal expected movement, consistent with the typical mean-reverting behavior seen in many financial or commodity series over very short windows. At the one-week and one-month horizons, I applied a slight positive bias reflecting any prevailing trend or drift in the underlying series, but kept the adjustment modest because strong directional conviction was not warranted by the available information.

The confidence interval widths expand in a way that reflects growing uncertainty as the time horizon lengthens, which is a standard feature of forecasting under uncertainty. At one day, the interval is relatively tight at roughly plus or minus 0.60 around the point estimate, reflecting that day-to-day volatility in most price or rate series of this magnitude is constrained. At one week, the interval widens to span about 2.6 units total, incorporating the compounding of daily fluctuations and the possibility of modest trend shifts. At one month, the interval widens further to roughly 5.4 units, accounting for the much larger range of possible paths the series could take over that period, including regime changes or sustained directional moves.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the upside, a sudden supply disruption, a hawkish policy surprise, or a sharp shift in sentiment could drive prices well above the upper bound of the one-month interval. On the downside, a demand shock, an unexpected easing in conditions, or a broad risk-off episode could push the series below the lower bound. At the one-day horizon, a major data release or geopolitical event occurring overnight would be the most likely catalyst for an outside move, which is difficult to anticipate in advance.

It is also worth acknowledging that my intervals assume a roughly symmetric distribution of outcomes around the point estimate, which may not always be appropriate. If the underlying series is subject to fat tails, skewness, or non-linear dynamics, actual extreme outcomes could materialize more frequently than my stated 90% confidence intervals would suggest. Structural breaks, liquidity events, or correlated shocks across markets represent the category of risk most likely to render my confidence bounds too narrow, particularly at the one-month horizon.
